question: Under the Navigation Rules' hierarchy of vessels, which vessel must generally keep out of the way of a vessel that is 'engaged in fishing' with gear (nets, lines, or trawls) that restricts its maneuverability?
choice_a: A power-driven vessel must generally keep out of the way of a vessel engaged in fishing
choice_b: The fishing vessel must always keep out of the way of a power-driven vessel
choice_c: Whichever vessel has right-of-way is decided by which one arrived at the fishing spot first
choice_d: Fishing vessels have no special status under the Navigation Rules
explanation: Rule 18 of the Navigation Rules establishes a hierarchy in which a power-driven vessel underway must keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, and a vessel engaged in fishing (with gear that restricts maneuverability).

question: Besides power-driven vessels, which other vessel type is also required by Rule 18 to keep out of the way of a vessel 'not under command,' a vessel 'restricted in her ability to maneuver,' and a vessel engaged in fishing?
choice_a: No other vessel type has this obligation; only power-driven vessels do
choice_b: A sailing vessel under sail alone
choice_c: Only vessels longer than 65 feet
choice_d: Only vessels operating at night
explanation: Rule 18 places sailing vessels below vessels not under command, vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver, and vessels engaged in fishing in the right-of-way hierarchy, meaning a sailing vessel must keep clear of those vessel types even though it generally has right-of-way over power-driven vessels.

question: What does the term 'vessel not under command' mean under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Any vessel that does not have a licensed captain aboard
choice_b: A vessel that is anchored for the night
choice_c: A vessel that, through some exceptional circumstance such as equipment failure, is unable to maneuver as the Rules require and therefore cannot keep out of the way of another vessel
choice_d: A vessel operating without a working horn
explanation: The Navigation Rules define a 'vessel not under command' as one which, due to an exceptional circumstance, is unable to maneuver as required by the Rules and is therefore unable to keep out of the way of another vessel -- for example, a boat with a disabled engine or steering failure.

question: Which of the following is an example of a vessel 'restricted in her ability to maneuver' under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Any personal watercraft (PWC) traveling faster than idle speed
choice_b: Any vessel more than 26 feet long
choice_c: Any vessel with more than one person aboard
choice_d: A vessel engaged in dredging, underwater survey work, or towing that severely restricts its ability to change course
explanation: The Navigation Rules list specific examples of vessels 'restricted in her ability to maneuver' due to the nature of their work, including vessels laying or servicing navigation marks, dredging or surveying, transferring persons or cargo while underway, and vessels towing another vessel or object in a way that severely restricts course changes.

question: Under the Navigation Rules, does a vessel trolling a fishing line (without gear that restricts its ability to maneuver) qualify as a 'vessel engaged in fishing' for right-of-way purposes?
choice_a: No -- vessels using trolling lines or other gear that does not restrict maneuverability are specifically excluded from the definition of 'vessel engaged in fishing'
choice_b: Yes -- any vessel with a line in the water automatically gets fishing-vessel priority
choice_c: Yes, but only on the Colorado River
choice_d: It depends on whether the angler has caught a fish that day
explanation: The Navigation Rules' definition of 'vessel engaged in fishing' covers vessels using nets, lines, trawls, or other apparatus that restricts maneuverability, but it specifically excludes vessels using trolling lines or other gear that does not restrict maneuverability -- so a boat simply trolling does not get the elevated right-of-way status of a fishing vessel.

question: How can an operator tell that a risk of collision exists with an approaching vessel, according to the Navigation Rules' guidance on assessing risk?
choice_a: Risk of collision only exists if the other vessel is sounding its horn
choice_b: If the compass bearing to the approaching vessel does not appreciably change over time as the range decreases, risk of collision should be deemed to exist
choice_c: Risk of collision can only be determined using radar; visual observation is not a valid method
choice_d: Risk of collision exists only when vessels are within 50 feet of each other
explanation: Rule 7 explains that a constant or nearly constant compass bearing to an approaching vessel, combined with decreasing range, indicates risk of collision exists; operators must use all available means, including visual bearing checks, to make this determination and should assume risk exists in doubtful cases.

question: What is the give-way vessel's specific duty under Rule 16 of the Navigation Rules once it is required to keep out of the way of another vessel?
choice_a: Wait until the last possible moment to react so the other vessel can plan its own course
choice_b: Sound its horn continuously until the other vessel moves
choice_c: Take early and substantial action to keep well clear of the other vessel
choice_d: Come to a complete stop regardless of the situation
explanation: Rule 16 requires that any vessel directed to keep out of the way of another vessel take early and substantial action, so far as possible, to keep well clear -- last-second or minor course changes do not satisfy this duty.

question: Under Rule 17, what may a stand-on vessel do if it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action to avoid a collision, even before a collision becomes imminent?
choice_a: The stand-on vessel must continue holding course and speed no matter what, until a collision is unavoidable
choice_b: The stand-on vessel is legally forbidden from changing course under any circumstances
choice_c: The stand-on vessel must radio the Coast Guard and wait for instructions before doing anything
choice_d: The stand-on vessel may take action to avoid collision by her own maneuver alone as soon as it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not acting appropriately
explanation: While the stand-on vessel should generally hold its course and speed, Rule 17 allows it to take avoiding action on its own as soon as it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action -- it does not have to wait until collision is truly imminent.

question: In conditions of restricted visibility such as fog, heavy rain, or haze, what speed and engine readiness does Rule 19 require of a power-driven vessel?
choice_a: Proceed at a safe speed adapted to the prevailing restricted-visibility conditions, with engines ready for immediate maneuvering
choice_b: Maintain full cruising speed so as to clear the area of poor visibility as quickly as possible
choice_c: Shut off the engine completely and drift until visibility improves
choice_d: Speed is not regulated in restricted visibility, only lighting requirements apply
explanation: Rule 19 requires every vessel to proceed at a safe speed adapted to restricted visibility, and a power-driven vessel must have its engines ready for immediate maneuver so it can respond quickly if another vessel is detected.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.19, Rule 19 (Conduct of Vessels in Restricted Visibility)

question: If an operator detects another vessel by radar alone (not visually) forward of the beam in restricted visibility and determines a close-quarters situation is developing, which action should generally be avoided, except when overtaking?
choice_a: Reducing speed
choice_b: Altering course to port for a vessel that is forward of the beam
choice_c: Sounding fog signals
choice_d: Monitoring the vessel's bearing over time
explanation: Rule 19 specifies that, except in an overtaking situation, an operator should avoid altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam when action is taken based on radar detection alone in restricted visibility, since this could bring the vessels closer together rather than apart.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.19, Rule 19 (Conduct of Vessels in Restricted Visibility)

question: If an operator in restricted visibility hears the fog signal of another vessel apparently forward of the beam and cannot avoid a close-quarters situation, what must the operator do?
choice_a: Increase speed to pass the area more quickly
choice_b: Turn on all deck lights and continue at the same speed
choice_c: Reduce speed to the minimum at which the vessel can be kept on course, taking all way off if necessary, and navigate with extreme caution until the danger of collision has passed
choice_d: Ignore the signal unless the other vessel is visible
explanation: Rule 19 requires that upon hearing what appears to be the fog signal of a vessel forward of the beam, or when a close-quarters situation cannot be avoided, an operator must reduce speed to the minimum needed to maintain steerage, take all way off if necessary, and proceed with extreme caution until clear of danger.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.19, Rule 19 (Conduct of Vessels in Restricted Visibility)

question: When navigating a narrow channel or fairway (such as a marked channel on a reservoir or the Colorado River), which side should a vessel generally keep to under Rule 9?
choice_a: The exact center of the channel at all times
choice_b: Whichever side has less boat traffic that day
choice_c: The outer limit on the vessel's own port (left) side
choice_d: As near to the outer limit of the channel or fairway that lies on the vessel's own starboard (right) side as is safe and practicable
explanation: Rule 9 requires a vessel proceeding along a narrow channel or fairway to keep as near to the outer limit of the channel that lies on her own starboard side as is safe and practicable, similar to keeping to the right on a road.

question: Under Rule 9, what obligation does a vessel under 20 meters or a sailing vessel have toward a larger vessel that can safely navigate only within a narrow channel?
choice_a: The smaller vessel or sailing vessel must not impede the larger vessel's safe passage within the narrow channel
choice_b: The larger vessel must always give way to any smaller vessel regardless of location
choice_c: There is no special obligation; normal crossing rules apply with no exception
choice_d: The smaller vessel has absolute right-of-way over all larger vessels in a channel
explanation: Rule 9 states that a vessel of less than 20 meters in length or a sailing vessel shall not impede the passage of a larger vessel that can safely navigate only within a narrow channel or fairway.

question: May a vessel cross a narrow channel or fairway under Rule 9?
choice_a: Crossing a narrow channel is completely prohibited under all circumstances
choice_b: A vessel shall not cross a narrow channel or fairway if doing so would impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within that channel
choice_c: A vessel may cross a narrow channel at any time as long as it sounds one horn blast first
choice_d: Only sailing vessels are permitted to cross narrow channels
explanation: Rule 9 does not forbid crossing a narrow channel outright, but it prohibits crossing in a way that impedes the passage of a vessel that can only navigate safely within that channel.

question: What must a power-driven vessel intending to overtake another vessel do while operating within a narrow channel, under Rule 9?
choice_a: Overtake silently to avoid startling the other vessel
choice_b: Wait until reaching open water outside the channel before overtaking is allowed at all
choice_c: Indicate its intention by sounding the appropriate signal, and the vessel being overtaken must take steps to permit safe passing if agreeing to be passed
choice_d: Pass only on the other vessel's port side, regardless of conditions
explanation: Rule 9 requires a vessel intending to overtake another in a narrow channel to indicate its intention with the appropriate sound signal, and if the overtaken vessel agrees the passage is safe, it must take steps to permit safe passing.

question: When approaching a bend in a narrow channel or an area where other vessels may be hidden from view (common on winding sections of the Colorado River), what does Rule 9 require?
choice_a: Speed up to clear the bend before another vessel can appear
choice_b: No special precautions are required as long as running lights are on
choice_c: Come to a complete stop before every bend
choice_d: Navigate with particular alertness and caution, and sound one prolonged blast to signal the approach
explanation: Rule 9 requires vessels approaching a bend or an area of a channel where other traffic may be obscured to navigate with particular alertness and caution, and to sound one prolonged blast to warn any vessel that may be hidden around the bend.

question: In a meeting or crossing situation, what does one short blast of a vessel's horn mean under the Navigation Rules' maneuvering and warning signals?
choice_a: 'I intend to leave you on my port side'
choice_b: 'I intend to leave you on my starboard side'
choice_c: 'I am operating astern propulsion'
choice_d: 'I am in distress and require assistance'
explanation: Under Rule 34, one short blast in a meeting or crossing situation signals 'I intend to leave you on my port side' (in an overtaking situation it instead means 'I intend to overtake you on your starboard side').

question: In a meeting or crossing situation, what does two short blasts of a vessel's horn mean under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: 'I intend to leave you on my port side'
choice_b: 'I intend to leave you on my starboard side'
choice_c: 'I am operating astern propulsion'
choice_d: 'I am altering my course to starboard'
explanation: Under Rule 34, two short blasts in a meeting or crossing situation signal 'I intend to leave you on my starboard side' (in an overtaking situation it instead means 'I intend to overtake you on your port side').

question: What does three short blasts of a vessel's horn mean under the Navigation Rules' maneuvering signals?
choice_a: 'I am altering course to port'
choice_b: 'I intend to overtake you'
choice_c: 'I am operating astern propulsion' (backing up)
choice_d: 'Danger -- I do not understand your intentions'
explanation: Rule 34 assigns three short blasts the meaning 'I am operating astern propulsion,' signaling that the vessel is moving in reverse.

question: What sound signal must an operator give if they are in doubt about another vessel's intentions, or believe the other vessel is not taking sufficient action to avoid collision?
choice_a: One long blast followed by silence
choice_b: Two short blasts only
choice_c: No signal is required; the operator should simply change course without warning
choice_d: At least five short and rapid blasts on the horn (the danger or doubt signal)
explanation: Rule 34 requires that when vessels are approaching each other and either operator fails to understand the other's intentions or actions, or is in doubt whether sufficient action is being taken to avoid collision, that operator must immediately sound the danger/doubt signal of at least five short and rapid blasts.

question: In restricted visibility such as fog, what sound signal must a power-driven vessel underway and making way through the water sound, and how often?
choice_a: One prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
choice_b: Two prolonged blasts every 30 seconds
choice_c: Five short blasts every minute
choice_d: No sound signal is required if the vessel has working running lights
explanation: Rule 35 requires a power-driven vessel making way through the water in restricted visibility to sound one prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35, Rule 35 (Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility)

question: In restricted visibility, what sound signal must a power-driven vessel underway but stopped and not making way through the water sound?
choice_a: One short blast every 10 seconds
choice_b: Two prolonged blasts in succession, with about a 2-second interval between them, repeated at intervals of not more than 2 minutes
choice_c: Continuous blasting until visibility improves
choice_d: No signal is required while stopped
explanation: Rule 35 requires a power-driven vessel that is underway but stopped and making no way through the water in restricted visibility to sound two prolonged blasts in succession, about 2 seconds apart, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes -- distinguishing it from a vessel still making way.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.35, Rule 35 (Sound Signals in Restricted Visibility)

question: Which set of navigation right-of-way rules governs boat traffic on Arizona's larger navigable waters, such as the Colorado River and reservoirs like Lake Mead, Lake Powell, and Lake Havasu?
choice_a: The International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea (COLREGS), which apply only on the open ocean
choice_b: Arizona has its own separate right-of-way rules that differ entirely from federal navigation rules
choice_c: The Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR Part 83), which apply to the inland waters of the United States
choice_d: No navigation rules apply on lakes and rivers, only on the ocean
explanation: The Inland Navigation Rules found in 33 CFR Part 83 apply to vessels on the inland waters of the United States, which includes Arizona's rivers and reservoirs such as the Colorado River, Lake Mead, Lake Powell, and Lake Havasu; the separate International Rules (COLREGS) apply seaward of the COLREGS demarcation lines near the coast.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.01, Rule 1 (Application); 33 CFR Part 80 (COLREGS Demarcation Lines)

question: Under Rule 8, what quality must an operator's action to avoid a collision have, if a course or speed change is made?
choice_a: The action can be as small as possible so as not to alarm the other operator
choice_b: Action should always be delayed until the vessels are within a few feet of each other
choice_c: Only a change in speed is acceptable; course changes are never allowed
choice_d: The action must be positive, made in ample time, and large enough to be readily apparent to the other vessel
explanation: Rule 8 requires that any action taken to avoid collision be positive, made in ample time, and observant of good seamanship; if altering course or speed, the change should be large enough to be readily apparent to another vessel observing visually or by radar, avoiding a succession of small changes.

question: Under Rule 18, which vessel type must a vessel engaged in fishing keep out of the way of?
choice_a: A vessel not under command and a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver
choice_b: All power-driven vessels, without exception
choice_c: All sailing vessels, without exception
choice_d: A fishing vessel has right-of-way over every other vessel type
explanation: Even a vessel engaged in fishing, which generally has priority over power-driven and sailing vessels, must still keep out of the way of a vessel not under command and a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, since those vessel types sit above it in Rule 18's hierarchy.
